name: Reporting Under More Than One Standard
title: Reporting Under More Than One Standard
answer: Reporting under more than one standard covers the work of presenting a single set of underlying transactions in two or more accounting frameworks at once, most often IFRS and US GAAP, and sometimes local statutory rules alongside a group standard. It sits inside financial reporting and synthesis, where the same ledger feeds a primary statement set, a reconciliation, and the disclosures each framework demands. The scope runs from a full dual-reporting close to narrower tasks such as converting one policy area, a lease portfolio or a revenue stream, for a filing or a lender pack.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Reporting under more than one standard covers the work of presenting a single set of underlying transactions in two or more accounting frameworks at once, most often IFRS and US GAAP, and sometimes local statutory rules alongside a group standard. It sits inside financial reporting and synthesis, where the same ledger feeds a primary statement set, a reconciliation, and the disclosures each framework demands. The scope runs from a full dual-reporting close to narrower tasks such as converting one policy area, a lease portfolio or a revenue stream, for a filing or a lender pack.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on the general ledger and its chart of accounts, a consolidation system that can hold more than one reporting hierarchy, and a mapping layer that ties each source account to its treatment under each standard. Spreadsheets still carry much of the reconciliation, though they are increasingly wrapped in controlled templates or replaced by tools that store the adjustments as data rather than as cells. Entity structures, intercompany rules and currency translation sit underneath, because a difference in consolidation scope changes the numbers before any policy difference is applied.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Practitioners start from one audited base ledger and record standard-specific adjustments as separate, labelled entries, so the path from one framework to the other can be walked in either direction. Each adjustment is tied to the policy that drives it, such as lease recognition, development cost capitalisation, inventory valuation or the treatment of share-based payment, and is documented with the paragraph reference and the calculation. Reconciliations are then built to explain the movement in equity and profit between the two sets, and the same adjustment log feeds the disclosure notes that describe the differences.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Control rests on keeping the two frameworks genuinely separate in the ledger while keeping them provably linked, with access rights, review sign-off and version history over every adjustment. Provenance matters because an auditor or regulator will ask which standard, which policy election and which source document produced a given number, and a spreadsheet with hardcoded overrides answers none of those questions well.Nothing here is accounting, legal or investment advice, and a reader should take their own professional guidance on any specific treatment.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction of travel is toward a single tagged data set that can be rendered into more than one framework on demand, rather than two parallel closes maintained by hand. Digital tagging and structured filing push in that direction, and so does the steady narrowing of the gap between IFRS and US GAAP on several major topics, though differences in leases, intangibles and financial instruments remain. The practical effect is that the reconciliation, not the second ledger, becomes the durable artefact, and the people who can explain a difference clearly become more valuable than the people who can produce a second set of numbers.
